name: Agate-Pinnacle
specific_features: Automated beacon (distress, navigation, or unknown purpose)
description: Agate-Pinnacle is a small rocky world defined by its extraordinary vertical relief, where low gravity has allowed mountain formations to reach heights that dwarf anything on higher-gravity worlds. The rock is predominantly banded agate, layered in concentric rings of color, chalky white and burnt orange and steel blue, that are exposed in cross-section by erosion. The tallest pinnacles rise over twenty kilometers above the mean surface, their summits in near-vacuum.

The thin atmosphere pools in the valleys and canyon floors, creating pockets of relatively dense air where moisture condenses and sound carries. Above the atmosphere line, the pinnacles stand in vacuum silence, their agate surfaces polished by micrometeorite bombardment to a waxy sheen. The color banding creates a natural beauty that has made images of the pinnacles famous across settled space.

Microbial life clings to existence in the lower valleys, sustained by chemical energy from subsurface mineral reactions. A navigational beacon was installed at the planet's highest point centuries ago, its signal a reference marker for shipping routes in the sector. The beacon has outlived its installers, an organization that no longer exists, and its maintenance is now performed by whoever happens to pass through and considers it worth the effort.

Agate-Pinnacle's scenic value has generated tourism interest, though the thin atmosphere and extreme terrain limit visitation to well-equipped expeditions. The banded agate is commercially valuable as a decorative stone, and small-scale quarrying operations have begun in the lower elevations. Conservationists argue that the pinnacles are a unique geological heritage site, but without formal protection, the quarriers continue to cut. Each slab removed is a layer of color that took millions of years to deposit.
